desc:
The array nums is sorted in non-decreasing order. Remove surplus copies so that every distinct value appears at most k times, keeping the remaining values in their original order. Return the resulting array.

nums = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], k = 2
result = [1, 1, 2, 2, 3]
nums = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3], k = 1
result = [0, 1, 2, 3]

Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra space by overwriting the array in place.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Since the array is sorted, equal values are adjacent. A value is a surplus copy when at least k copies of it were already kept.
Keep a write pointer w: the number of elements kept so far. The kept prefix is itself sorted, so the last k kept elements tell you how many copies of the current value you already hold.
Accept nums[i] if w < k or nums[i] != nums[w - k]; in that case write it at nums[w] and increment w. If nums[w - k] already equals the value, then all k kept elements after it are equal too.
editorial: Scan with a read index i and keep the result in the prefix nums[0:w]. When we consider x = nums[i], the kept prefix is sorted and its last element is at most x. The number of kept copies of x is at least k exactly when nums[w - k] == x (the element k places before the end of the kept prefix is equal to x, and everything between them is sandwiched, so equal too).

Therefore x is accepted iff w < k or nums[w - k] != x. This one-line test is the whole algorithm and it works for every k without a separate counter; for k = 1 it is the classic dedup and for k = 2 the 'at most twice' version.
Each element is read once and written at most once: O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
